title: Funny String
directAnswer: Build the list of absolute differences between adjacent characters, |s[i] − s[i−1]|. Do the same for the reversed string. The string is 'funny' when those two difference lists are identical. The clean trick: you don't have to physically reverse the string — the reverse's difference at position i equals the original's difference read from the opposite end. Compare s's differences front-to-back against the same list back-to-front. O(n) time, O(1) space.

rules: Compare **absolute** differences — `|s[i] − s[i−1]|`, never the signed value.
You don't need to allocate `reverse(s)`: the reversed difference at step `i` is `|s[n−i] − s[n−i−1]|`.
Index the original characters by their **ASCII / code-point** value, not the character itself.
Loop `i` from `1` to `n−1`; both the forward and mirrored differences are valid in that range.
Any single mismatch ends it as 'Not Funny'; survive all positions and it's 'Funny'.
whenToUse: You must compare a string's adjacent-difference profile against its reverse
The property is defined on gaps between neighbours, not the characters themselves
You want to avoid building the reversed string and just mirror the index
A symmetry / palindrome-of-differences check is hidden inside the prompt
antiSignals: The property uses the characters directly (not gaps) → compare characters, not differences
Signed direction matters → don't take absolute value
You must transform the string, not just answer yes/no → you may actually need the reverse
Differences are over non-adjacent pairs → it's no longer a simple neighbour scan
remember.takeaway: A string is funny exactly when its sequence of adjacent absolute differences is a palindrome. Reversing the string reverses that difference sequence, so 'equal to its reverse's differences' is the same as 'the difference sequence reads the same both ways'. Mirror the index instead of building the reverse to keep it O(1) space.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you translate the wordy definition into a concrete invariant — the adjacent absolute-difference sequence — and whether you realise reversing the string just reverses that sequence, so no extra allocation is needed.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Comparing the characters of s and its reverse instead of the differences, or forgetting the absolute value so a negative gap fails to match its positive mirror.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the insight out loud: 'funny' means the difference sequence is a palindrome. Then skip building reverse(s) entirely by mirroring the index, turning O(n) extra space into O(1).

problemStatement:
A string is **funny** if, comparing it with its reverse, the absolute difference between the ASCII values of every pair of adjacent characters is preserved.

Formally, let `r = reverse(s)`. For every position `i` from `1` to `|s| − 1`, the string is funny if `|s[i] − s[i−1]| == |r[i] − r[i−1]|`, where `s[i]` denotes the ASCII value of the character.

Return `"Funny"` if the condition holds for all `i`, and `"Not Funny"` otherwise.
constraints: s consists of lowercase (or mixed) English letters
Differences are taken over ASCII / code-point values
understanding: Forget the characters themselves; what matters is the gap between each pair of neighbours. Slide a window of size two across the string and record |gap|. Do the same on the reverse. The string is funny when those two gap profiles line up exactly. Because reversing a string reverses its gap profile, 'matches the reverse' is just 'the gap profile is a palindrome'.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Absolute difference or signed?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Absolute. The definition uses |s[i] − s[i−1]|, so direction is discarded.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I need to actually build the reversed string?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. The reverse's adjacent difference at step i equals |s[n−i] − s[n−i−1]| in the original, so you can mirror the index and stay O(1) space.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What counts as the value of a character?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Its ASCII / Unicode code point. In Java a char is already an int; in Python use ord().

clarifyingQuestions.question: What about a single-character or empty string?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: There are no adjacent pairs, so the condition is vacuously true → 'Funny'. The loop simply never runs.

examples.explanation: Forward gaps: |c−a|=2, |x−c|=21, |z−x|=2 → [2,21,2]. Reverse 'zxca' gaps: |x−z|=2, |c−x|=21, |a−c|=2 → [2,21,2]. They match.
Forward gaps: |c−b|=1, |x−c|=21, |z−x|=2 → [1,21,2]. Reverse gaps: [2,21,1]. First positions differ (1 vs 2).
No adjacent pairs exist, so the condition holds vacuously.

approaches.name: Build the Reverse and Compare Difference Lists (Baseline)
approaches.whenToMention: Open with this — it follows the definition literally and is easy to get right, then note the extra O(n) space.
hints: The definition mentions reverse(s) explicitly. What's the most direct way to follow it?
Physically reverse the string, then build two arrays of adjacent absolute differences — one for s, one for the reverse.
Compare the two difference arrays element by element; equal everywhere means 'Funny'.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Reversing is O(n), building each difference list is O(n), and comparing them is O(n) → O(n) time. Storing the reversed string and/or two difference arrays costs O(n) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
Follow the wording of the problem to the letter: form `r = reverse(s)`, compute the adjacent absolute differences of both strings, and check the two lists are identical.

**Why it is correct by construction.** The problem defines 'funny' as 'the adjacent difference profiles of `s` and `reverse(s)` agree'. This approach computes exactly those two profiles and compares them, so there is no room for an off-by-one in the *logic* — only in the indexing.

**Why absolute value is essential.** `|s[i] − s[i−1]|` discards sign. If you kept the signed difference, the reverse would flip every sign (walking the same neighbours in the opposite direction), and almost nothing would ever be funny. Taking the absolute value is what makes the forward and mirrored gaps comparable.

**Why we don't ship it.** It allocates a reversed string and (often) two difference arrays — `O(n)` memory — to answer a yes/no question. The reverse's difference at position `i` is fully determined by the original string, so we can compute it on the fly and drop all the extra storage. Use this version to make the definition concrete, then fold it into the index-mirroring solution.
approaches.insight: Writing out both difference lists makes the symmetry obvious: the reverse's list is literally s's list read backwards. That observation is the bridge to the O(1)-space version — you never needed the reversed string, only its differences, which you already have.

dryRun.intro: Reverse to 'zxca', build both gap lists, then compare.

java.explanation: Physically build the reverse — the O(n) allocation we'll later eliminate.
char subtraction promotes to int; abs() discards direction.
Any mismatch between forward and reverse gaps disqualifies the string.

python.explanation: Slice-reverse builds a whole new string — O(n) extra space.
ord() gives the code point; abs() takes the magnitude of the gap.

pitfalls: Comparing characters of s and r instead of their adjacent differences.
Dropping the absolute value, so signed gaps never match across the reverse.
Allocating the reversed string when an index mirror would do.

approaches.name: Mirror the Index — No Reverse Allocated (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The polished answer. Phrase it as 'the reverse's gap at i is just s's gap read from the other end'.
hints: You built reverse(s) only to read its adjacent differences. Can you express the reverse's difference at position i purely in terms of s?
In the reverse, position i holds s[n-1-i]. So |r[i] - r[i-1]| = |s[n-1-i] - s[n-i]| = |s[n-i] - s[n-i-1]| in the original.
Loop i from 1 to n-1, compare |s[i] - s[i-1]| against |s[n-i] - s[n-i-1]|. No reversed string, no difference arrays — just two subtractions per step.
approaches.complexityReasoning: A single pass with i from 1 to n−1 does O(1) work per step → O(n) time. You hold only a couple of integers, so O(1) extra space — no reversed string, no arrays.
approaches.explanation:
Walk one index `i` from `1` to `n−1`. At each step compare the forward gap `|s[i] − s[i−1]|` with the *mirrored* gap `|s[n−i] − s[n−i−1]|`. If they ever disagree, return 'Not Funny'; survive the whole range and return 'Funny'.

**Where the mirror index comes from.** In the reversed string `r`, character at position `i` is the original character at position `n−1−i`. So the reverse's adjacent gap `|r[i] − r[i−1]|` equals `|s[n−1−i] − s[n−1−(i−1)]| = |s[n−1−i] − s[n−i]|`. Since absolute value ignores order, that's `|s[n−i] − s[n−i−1]|`. The reverse's gap at step `i` is therefore a plain expression in the *original* string — no `r` required.

**Why this is the same test as the baseline.** The baseline compared two lists; this compares the same two values pairwise, just sourced directly from `s`. As `i` runs forward, the mirror index `n−i` runs backward, so we're checking `s`'s gap sequence against itself reversed — exactly the palindrome-of-differences condition.

**Why absolute value still matters.** Reading the neighbours from the opposite end swaps which one is subtracted first, flipping the sign. The absolute value erases that flip so the forward and mirrored gaps are directly comparable. Drop it and the mirror almost never matches.

**Why O(1) space.** The only state is the loop counter and two freshly computed integer gaps per iteration. Nothing scales with `n`, so memory is constant — the entire reason to prefer this over the baseline.

**Why early exit is safe.** A single position where the forward and mirrored gaps differ is a witness that the difference sequence is not a palindrome, which is enough to conclude 'Not Funny' without scanning the rest.
approaches.insight: Whenever you only need a transformed string's *derived* values (here, adjacent gaps) rather than the string itself, look for a closed-form index map back into the original. Reverse maps position `i` to `n−1−i`; substituting that turns an O(n)-space copy into O(1)-space arithmetic.

dryRun.intro: n = 4. Compare forward gap at i with mirrored gap |s[n-i] - s[n-i-1]|.

java.explanation: i indexes forward gaps; for each, n-i indexes the mirrored gap from the far end.
Gap between this character and its left neighbour in the original direction.

java.line: int mirror = Math.abs(s.charAt(n - i) - s.charAt(n - i - 1));
java.explanation: The reverse's gap at step i, rewritten in terms of s — no reversed string needed.
A single disagreement breaks the palindrome-of-differences and ends the scan.

python.explanation: Forward index; mirror index n-i walks inward from the right simultaneously.
Magnitude of the gap to the previous character.
Reverse's gap expressed directly on s via the n-i mirror — O(1) space.

diagrams.title: Forward gap vs mirrored gap
diagrams.caption: i scans gaps left-to-right; the mirror gap is read from the right end using n-i.

edgeCases.behavior: n = 1, loop from 1 never runs → 'Funny' (no adjacent pairs to violate).
fwd |b-a|=1, mirror also |b-a|=1 (mirror reads s[1],s[0]) → 'Funny'; any 2-char string is funny.

pitfalls: Off-by-one on the mirror: it's s[n-i] and s[n-i-1], not s[n-1-i] alone.
Forgetting abs(), so the sign flip from reading right-to-left breaks the match.
Subtracting characters without code-point semantics (fine in Java; use ord() in Python).

commonMistakes: Comparing the characters of s and its reverse rather than the adjacent differences.
Using signed differences instead of absolute values.
Getting the mirror index wrong when avoiding an explicit reverse.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Comparing characters, not differences
commonMistakesDetailed.why: 'Funny' is about the GAPS between neighbours, not the letters. Comparing s[i] to r[i] tests whether the string is a palindrome — a different, stricter property.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Dropping the absolute value
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Reading neighbours from the reversed end flips the sign of every gap. Without abs() the forward gap +2 never equals the reverse gap −2, so almost no string is judged funny.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong mirror index
commonMistakesDetailed.why: When skipping the explicit reverse, the reverse's gap at step i is |s[n-i] - s[n-i-1]|. Using s[n-1-i] for a single character (instead of the pair) silently compares the wrong neighbours.

patternNote: Difference-sequence symmetry. Translate a wordy string property into a concrete invariant — here the sequence of adjacent absolute differences — then notice that reversing the string reverses that sequence, so the test becomes 'is the difference sequence a palindrome?'. Mirroring the index (i ↔ n−i) reads the reverse's values straight off the original, trading O(n) space for O(1).
